writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only variable-window program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
On [2,3,1,2,4,3] with target 7, expanding reaches a valid sum, then shrinking removes unnecessary left values. Near the end, [4,3] reaches 7 with length 2. Negative values would invalidate this simple monotone rule.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: For positive values, return the minimum length with sum at least 7. The visible fixture is `[2,3,1,2,4,3]` and its example result is `2`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Variable-Size Window when it asks for minimum or maximum contiguous ranges under a monotone constraint. Here the concrete task is: For positive values, return the minimum length with sum at least 7. The visible input `[2,3,1,2,4,3]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Choose this family when a valid window can be repaired by moving one boundary; non-monotone constraints may need a different method. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Expand until a constraint fails, then shrink until it is valid again. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A window is a contiguous interval with a maintained summary. Describe what entering the right edge adds and what leaving the left edge removes. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(1) or state space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `2` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test an empty window, a window spanning the whole input, and a case where the left edge must advance several times. Represent bounds as a half-open range when possible. Keep counts and the window length in sync when shrinking it. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
